error_modes.label: ALTITUDE CONTROL THROUGH THE PITCH OUT

texts.0: SP, due to attention held outside on the leader instead of returning to the altimeter after the roll-in, did not maintain the pitch out altitude and allowed the aircraft to descend throughout the turn. The aircraft passed 400 feet below the pattern altitude with the descent still developing and no correction started. IP took the controls and recovered the aircraft to the pattern altitude before rollout on downwind.
texts.1: SP, due to a pitch attitude that was not reset against the bank after establishing the pitch out, did not hold the pitch out altitude and let the aircraft settle in the turn. The deviation reached 300 feet low, at the limit of the tolerance for the maneuver, and stopped only after IP called the altitude twice. SP regained the pattern altitude on downwind, but the correction came from verbal prompting rather than from own cross-check.
texts.2: SP, due to a delayed return of the cross-check to the altimeter after rolling into the pitch out, initially allowed the aircraft to descend about 200 feet below the pattern altitude. SP identified the deviation while still in the turn and corrected back inside the tolerance before rolling out on downwind. No prompting or intervention by IP was required.
texts.3: SP maintained the pitch out altitude throughout the turn with deviations contained inside 150 feet. The altimeter cross-check ran continuously against the bank and the aircraft was level at the pattern altitude at rollout on downwind. Corrections were small, early and made on SP own initiative.
texts.4: SP flew the pitch out with the altitude held essentially constant, the deviation never exceeding a few tens of feet at any point in the turn. Pitch was traded against bank with no perceptible settle at either the roll-in or the rollout. The pattern altitude was regained and held with negligible error.
texts.marginal: SP maintained the pitch out altitude within standards, but every turn was flown with the same low bias, reaching about 130 feet before being corrected on the downwind leg. The trend is a repeated settle at the roll-in that is caught late instead of being prevented. SP is expected to set and hold the pitch attitude against the bank as it is established, so that the altitude stays within a considerably tighter band.

texts_at.0: SP flew the pitch out with the IP calling the pitch attitude needed against the bank as the turn was established. Setting and holding the pitch attitude against the bank at the roll-in is a first exposure at this stage, so the compensation is not yet applied without a cue. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to set and hold the pitch attitude against the bank as it is established, so the altitude stays within a considerably tighter band.
texts_at.1: SP, due to a pitch attitude not reset against the bank after establishing the pitch out, let the aircraft settle in the turn to the 300 foot limit before the pattern altitude was regained on downwind. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to set and hold the pitch attitude against the bank as it is established, so the altitude stays within a considerably tighter band.
texts_at.2: SP, due to a delayed return of the cross-check to the altimeter after rolling into the pitch out, allowed the aircraft to descend about 200 feet below the pattern altitude before identifying the deviation and correcting back inside tolerance while still in the turn. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to set and hold the pitch attitude against the bank as it is established, so the altitude stays within a considerably tighter band.
texts_at.3: SP, due to a brief lag in returning the cross-check to the altimeter after roll-in, maintained the pitch out altitude with deviations contained near 150 feet, with the altimeter cross-check running against the bank for nearly the whole turn. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to set and hold the pitch attitude against the bank as it is established, so the altitude stays within a considerably tighter band.

texts_above.1: SP held the pitch out altitude to about 300 feet low as the turn settled, regaining the pattern altitude on downwind after a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP let the aircraft descend about 200 feet below the pattern altitude before identifying the deviation while still in the turn and correcting back inside tolerance before rollout on downwind, without prompting. Returning the cross-check to the altimeter as the roll-in is made, rather than after it, would hold that descent smaller. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good pitch-attitude-against-bank technique.
texts_above.3: SP maintained the pitch out altitude throughout the turn with deviations contained inside about 100 feet, the altimeter cross-check running continuously against the bank. The cross-check against the bank is already continuous; only the smallest further margin remains. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good pitch-attitude-against-bank technique.
texts_above.4: SP flew the pitch out with the altitude held essentially constant, the deviation never exceeding a few tens of feet at any point in the turn. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to excellent pitch-attitude-against-bank technique.

error_modes.label: AIRSPEED CONTROL DURING THE PITCH OUT

texts.0: SP, due to power left at the transit setting when the pitch out was executed, did not maintain the pre-determined airspeed required of formation members during the pitch out. The aircraft accelerated to 35 knots above the briefed figure and the excess was still increasing on downwind. IP had to direct the power reduction and then reduce the power personally to bring the aircraft back inside the pattern speed.
texts.1: SP, due to the power reduction being made only after the bank was fully established rather than with it, did not hold the pre-determined pitch out airspeed. The aircraft reached 20 knots fast, at the limit of the tolerance, and was brought back only after IP called the airspeed. The speed was inside standards on downwind, but the correction was produced by the prompt and not by SP own scan.
texts.2: SP, due to a power setting selected without reference to the briefed pitch out figure, initially allowed the airspeed to build about 15 knots above the pre-determined value. SP noted the trend on the airspeed indicator during the turn and reset the power in good time, recovering the briefed speed before rollout on downwind without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP maintained the pre-determined pitch out airspeed with deviations contained inside 10 knots throughout the maneuver. Power was reduced together with the roll-in and adjusted in small increments as the bank was held. The briefed pattern speed was established on downwind without any correction being called.
texts.4: SP flew the pitch out with the airspeed pinned to the pre-determined figure, the deviation remaining within a very few knots from roll-in to rollout. Power was led rather than chased, so no speed excursion ever developed. The pattern speed on downwind was exactly the briefed value.
texts.marginal: SP held the pitch out airspeed within standards, but the aircraft was consistently about 9 knots fast from the roll-in to the rollout on downwind. The trend is a habitual late power reduction that leaves the speed at the outer edge of the acceptable band on every pitch out. SP is expected to reduce power together with the roll-in so that the pre-determined airspeed is achieved from the start of the turn.

texts_at.0: SP flew the pitch out with the IP calling the power reduction needed as the bank was established. Reducing power together with the roll-in, rather than after bank is established, is a first exposure at this stage, so the timing is not yet automatic. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to reduce power together with the roll-in so the pre-determined airspeed is achieved from the start of the turn.
texts_at.1: SP, due to a power reduction made only after the bank was fully established, reached 20 knots fast, at the limit of the tolerance, before the airspeed was brought back on the downwind leg. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to reduce power together with the roll-in so the pre-determined airspeed is achieved from the start of the turn.
texts_at.2: SP, due to a power setting selected without reference to the briefed pitch out figure, let the airspeed build about 15 knots above the pre-determined value before noting the trend and resetting power in good time, without prompting. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to reduce power together with the roll-in so the pre-determined airspeed is achieved from the start of the turn.
texts_at.3: SP, due to a brief lag in resetting power to the briefed figure, maintained the pre-determined pitch out airspeed with deviations contained near 10 knots, power reduced together with the roll-in. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to reduce power together with the roll-in so the pre-determined airspeed is achieved from the start of the turn.

texts_above.1: SP held the pitch out airspeed to about 20 knots fast before it was brought back on the downwind leg after a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP let the airspeed build about 15 knots above the pre-determined value before noting the trend on the indicator during the turn and resetting power in good time, recovering the briefed speed before rollout without prompting. Reducing power with the roll-in itself, rather than after it, would hold that build-up smaller. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to sound power-lead technique through the roll-in.
texts_above.3: SP maintained the pre-determined pitch out airspeed with deviations contained inside about 7 knots throughout the maneuver, power reduced together with the roll-in and adjusted in small increments. The power lead into the roll-in is already close; only the smallest margin remains to tighten. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to sure-handed power-lead technique through the roll-in.
texts_above.4: SP flew the pitch out with the airspeed pinned to the pre-determined figure, the deviation remaining within a very few knots from roll-in to rollout. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to exceptional power-lead technique through the roll-in.

error_modes.label: EXIT HEADING AND ROLLOUT ON DOWNWIND

texts.0: SP, due to the rollout being flown by looking at the runway rather than by anticipating the downwind heading, did not stop the turn on the required exit heading. The aircraft rolled out 18 degrees through the downwind heading and continued to diverge from the runway track. IP directed the recovery turn and then took the controls to reestablish the aircraft on the downwind leg.
texts.1: SP, due to the roll-out being started at the exit heading instead of being led, did not achieve the required exit heading of the pitch out. The aircraft settled 10 degrees off the downwind heading, at the limit of the tolerance, and was realigned only after IP called the heading. The correction restored the track but was produced by the prompt rather than by SP own cross-check.
texts.2: SP, due to a roll rate that was reduced too late in the recovery from the pitch out bank, initially rolled out about 8 degrees off the required downwind heading. SP recognized the offset immediately on the heading indicator and corrected onto the exit heading inside the tolerance before the spacing check, without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP rolled out of the pitch out on the required exit heading with the deviation contained inside 5 degrees. The roll-out was led so that the wings came level as the downwind heading was reached. The aircraft was tracking the downwind leg without any subsequent heading correction.
texts.4: SP stopped the pitch out precisely on the required exit heading, with the residual deviation of the order of one or two degrees. The roll-out was anticipated exactly, so the wings came level and the heading stabilized in the same instant. No corrective input was needed on the downwind leg.
texts.marginal: SP achieved the exit heading of the pitch out within standards, but every rollout finished about 5 degrees outside the downwind heading in the same direction. The trend is a roll-out that is consistently started late and then patched with a small corrective turn. SP is expected to lead the roll-out from the pitch out bank so that the exit heading is achieved directly rather than corrected afterwards.

texts_at.0: SP flew the roll-out to the downwind heading with the IP calling the heading to hold as the recovery from bank was made. Leading the roll-out from the pitch out bank is a first exposure at this stage, so the exit heading is not yet captured without a cue. The maneuver is being introduced at this point of the syllabus, so no independent standard is required yet. SP is expected to lead the roll-out from the pitch out bank so the exit heading is achieved directly rather than corrected afterwards.
texts_at.1: SP, due to the roll-out started at the exit heading instead of being led, settled 10 degrees off the downwind heading before the aircraft was realigned. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to lead the roll-out from the pitch out bank so the exit heading is achieved directly rather than corrected afterwards.
texts_at.2: SP, due to a roll rate reduced too late in the recovery from the pitch out bank, rolled out about 8 degrees off the required downwind heading before recognizing the offset on the heading indicator and correcting onto the exit heading inside tolerance. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to lead the roll-out from the pitch out bank so the exit heading is achieved directly rather than corrected afterwards.
texts_at.3: SP, due to a brief lag in reducing the roll rate during the recovery, rolled out of the pitch out on the required exit heading with the deviation contained near 5 degrees, the roll-out led so the wings came level as the downwind heading was reached. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to lead the roll-out from the pitch out bank so the exit heading is achieved directly rather than corrected afterwards.

texts_above.1: SP rolled out of the pitch out with the heading held to about 10 degrees off the downwind heading before the aircraft was realigned after a verbal call from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP rolled out about 8 degrees off the required downwind heading before recognizing the offset on the heading indicator and correcting onto the exit heading inside tolerance before the spacing check, without prompting. Reducing the roll rate earlier in the recovery would hold that offset smaller. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to solid roll-out lead technique on exit heading.
texts_above.3: SP rolled out of the pitch out on the required exit heading with the deviation contained inside about 3 degrees, the roll-out led so the wings came level as the downwind heading was reached. The roll-out is already led from the pitch out bank; only the smallest further margin remains. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to well-developed roll-out lead technique on exit heading.
texts_above.4: SP stopped the pitch out precisely on the required exit heading, with the residual deviation of the order of one or two degrees and the roll-out anticipated exactly. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to outstanding roll-out lead technique on exit heading.

error_modes.label: RESPONSE TO LEADER COMMAND AND PITCH OUT TIMING

texts.0: SP, due to the pitch out signal being expected on the radio while the leader gave it visually, did not execute the pitch out following the leader command as laid down in the Techniques and Procedures Manual. The turn was started more than eight seconds late and the resulting interval was far outside anything usable for the pattern. IP had to command the turn and then intervene on the controls to salvage a workable spacing.
texts.1: SP, due to hesitation in confirming the leader command before acting on it, did not execute the pitch out in a timely manner. The turn was initiated some three seconds late and the interval finished at the outer limit of what the pattern allows, being adjusted only after IP called for the turn. The maneuver was completed to standard, but the timing was driven by IP prompting.
texts.2: SP, due to the head being inside the cockpit at the moment the leader command was given, initially started the pitch out slightly late. SP recognized the delay at once, adjusted the bank and the power inside the briefed limits, and restored the interval to the required value before the downwind spacing check without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP executed the pitch out following the leader command, in the manner prescribed by the Techniques and Procedures Manual. The turn was started without perceptible delay and the resulting interval was the briefed one. No adjustment to the timing was required at any stage.
texts.4: SP executed the pitch out on the leader command with immediate and precise response, the turn starting exactly on the signal. The interval produced matched the briefed figure with negligible error and required no subsequent adjustment. SP anticipation of the command point was evident throughout.
texts.marginal: SP executed the pitch out following the leader command within standards, but consistently a beat behind the signal on each repetition. The trend is an interval built slightly long every time, absorbed later by adjustments on the downwind leg. SP is expected to act on the leader command as it is given so that the interval is correct from the roll-in.

texts_at.0: SP flew the pitch out with the IP calling the moment of the leader's command as the visual or radio signal was given. Reading the leader's command as it is given, rather than after a delay, is a first exposure at this stage, so the response is not yet automatic without a cue. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance. SP is expected to act on the leader command as it is given so the interval is correct from the roll-in.
texts_at.1: SP, due to the pitch out signal expected on the radio while the leader gave it visually, started the pitch out about eight seconds late, with the resulting interval reaching the outer limit of what the pattern allows before it was brought back to a usable value. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to act on the leader command as it is given so the interval is correct from the roll-in.
texts_at.2: SP, due to hesitation in confirming the leader command before acting on it, initiated the turn about three seconds late before recognizing the delay and adjusting bank and power within the briefed limits to restore the interval, without prompting. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to act on the leader command as it is given so the interval is correct from the roll-in.
texts_at.3: SP, due to a brief hesitation in confirming the leader command before acting on it, executed the pitch out following the leader command as prescribed by the Techniques and Procedures Manual, with the turn started without perceptible delay and the resulting interval the briefed one. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to act on the leader command as it is given so the interval is correct from the roll-in.

texts_above.1: SP executed the pitch out following the leader's command, starting the turn about three seconds late before the interval was restored after a verbal call from the IP. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP started the pitch out a little late after the head was inside the cockpit at the moment the command was given, then recognized the delay at once, adjusting bank and power within the briefed limits to restore the interval before the downwind spacing check, without prompting. Watching for the leader's command through the cockpit scan, rather than after it, would remove that delay. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady leader-command response timing.
texts_above.3: SP executed the pitch out following the leader command, in the manner prescribed by the Techniques and Procedures Manual, with the turn started without perceptible delay and no adjustment to the timing required. The response to the command is already close to immediate; only the smallest further margin remains. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate leader-command response timing.
texts_above.4: SP executed the pitch out on the leader command with immediate and precise response, the turn starting exactly on the signal and the interval matching the briefed figure with negligible error. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exemplary leader-command response timing.

texts.0: SP, due to the briefed bank value not being flown against the attitude indicator, did not maintain the pre-determined bank required of formation members during the pitch out. The bank was some 20 degrees shallower than briefed and the spacing produced was unusable for the pattern. IP took the controls, reestablished the correct bank and rebuilt the interval before the downwind leg.
texts.1: SP, due to a bank that was allowed to relax as attention moved back to the leader, did not hold the pre-determined pitch out bank. The bank wandered around the briefed value and the resulting spacing finished at the limit of what the pattern allows, being corrected only after IP called the bank angle. The interval was recovered, but through prompting rather than through SP own cross-check.
texts.2: SP, due to a roll-in that was stopped short of the briefed value, initially flew the pitch out with insufficient bank and a spacing trend toward the long side. SP identified the shallow bank on the attitude indicator early in the turn, increased it to the pre-determined value and restored the interval inside acceptable limits without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP maintained the pre-determined bank throughout the pitch out and produced the briefed spacing. The bank was set at the roll-in and held constant until the roll-out was led for the exit heading. The interval on downwind matched the briefed figure with no adjustment required.
texts.4: SP held the pre-determined pitch out bank with negligible variation from roll-in to roll-out, producing spacing that matched the briefed interval exactly. The bank was established in a single positive input and required no trimming during the turn. The resulting interval needed no correction whatsoever on the downwind leg.
texts.marginal: SP flew the pitch out with the pre-determined bank within standards, but the bank was consistently a few degrees shallow and the interval consistently at the long end of the acceptable range. The trend is a spacing that is workable but always has to be closed later in the pattern. SP is expected to set the full briefed bank at the roll-in so that the interval is generated by the pitch out itself.

texts_at.0: SP flew the pitch out with the IP calling the bank angle needed to generate the briefed spacing. Setting the full briefed bank at the roll-in, rather than adjusting into it, is a first exposure at this stage, so the bank is not yet set without a cue. The Training Section still expects IP assistance for this maneuver at this point. SP is expected to set the full briefed bank at the roll-in so the interval is generated by the pitch out itself.
texts_at.1: SP, due to a bank allowed to relax as attention moved back to the leader, let the bank wander around the briefed value, with the resulting spacing reaching the limit of what the pattern allows before the bank angle was reset and the interval recovered. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to set the full briefed bank at the roll-in so the interval is generated by the pitch out itself.
texts_at.2: SP, due to a roll-in stopped short of the briefed bank value, flew the pitch out with insufficient bank at first and a spacing trend toward the long side, before identifying the shallow bank on the attitude indicator, increasing it to the pre-determined value and restoring the interval without prompting. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to set the full briefed bank at the roll-in so the interval is generated by the pitch out itself.
texts_at.3: SP, due to a brief lag before the full briefed bank was established at the roll-in, maintained the pre-determined bank throughout the pitch out and produced the briefed spacing, the bank set at the roll-in and held constant until the roll-out was led. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to set the full briefed bank at the roll-in so the interval is generated by the pitch out itself.

texts_above.1: SP held the pre-determined bank through the pitch out, settling the spacing at the limit of the pattern before the bank angle was reset after a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP flew the pitch out with insufficient bank at first and a spacing trend toward the long side, before identifying the shallow bank on the attitude indicator, increasing it to the pre-determined value and restoring the interval inside acceptable limits without prompting. Setting the full bank at the roll-in itself, rather than adding to it afterward, would remove that early shortfall. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to dependable roll-in bank commitment.
texts_above.3: SP maintained the pre-determined bank throughout the pitch out and produced the briefed spacing, with the bank set at the roll-in and held constant until the roll-out was led for the exit heading. The bank is already set correctly at the roll-in; only the smallest further margin remains. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to notably good roll-in bank commitment.
texts_above.4: SP held the pre-determined pitch out bank with negligible variation from roll-in to roll-out, producing spacing that matched the briefed interval exactly. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to superior roll-in bank commitment.

error_modes.label: SMOOTHNESS AND SOLIDITY OF AIRCRAFT CONTROL

texts.0: SP, due to control inputs applied in large uncoordinated steps rather than in a continuous manner, did not control the aircraft in a smooth and solid way during the pitch out. The roll-in was abrupt, the ball was displaced for the whole turn and the load factor oscillated noticeably. IP took the controls to stabilize the aircraft and complete the maneuver.
texts.1: SP, due to overcontrolling in roll and then chasing the resulting pitch changes, did not fly the pitch out in a smooth and solid way. The turn was flown with repeated coarse corrections in roll and pitch and settled down only after IP called for smaller inputs. Control of the aircraft was regained, but only on verbal direction from IP.
texts.2: SP, due to a rudder input that did not accompany the initial roll, initially flew the pitch out out of balance with a visible ball displacement. SP recognized the uncoordinated entry, coordinated the rudder with the aileron and flew the remainder of the turn smoothly and firmly without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP controlled the aircraft in a smooth and solid way throughout the pitch out. Roll, pitch and rudder inputs were coordinated, the flight path was continuous and the aircraft remained in balance from entry to rollout. No coarse or corrective input was observed.
texts.4: SP flew the pitch out with control inputs of exceptional smoothness and precision, the aircraft tracking a continuous flight path with the ball centered throughout. Roll-in and roll-out were single positive movements with no subsequent correction. Any deviation from the ideal flight path was negligible.
texts.marginal: SP controlled the aircraft in a smooth and solid way within standards, but the roll rate at the entry varied noticeably between repetitions and small ball displacements appeared at each roll-out. The trend is inconsistency in the entry and exit inputs rather than any loss of control. SP is expected to standardize the roll rate and coordinate the rudder so that every pitch out is flown to the same smooth pattern.

texts_at.0: SP flew the pitch out with the IP calling for the rudder to be coordinated with the initial roll input. Coordinating rudder with the first roll input of a pitch out is a first exposure at this stage, so the coordination is not yet built without a cue. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to standardize the roll rate and coordinate the rudder so every pitch out is flown to the same smooth pattern.
texts_at.1: SP, due to overcontrolling in roll followed by chasing the resulting pitch changes, flew the turn with repeated coarse corrections in roll and pitch, letting the altitude run 300 feet low at the tolerance limit, before it settled down and control was regained. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to standardize the roll rate and coordinate the rudder so every pitch out is flown to the same smooth pattern.
texts_at.2: SP, due to a rudder input that did not accompany the initial roll, flew the pitch out out of balance with a visible ball displacement at first and let the altitude drop about 200 feet below the pattern altitude, before recognizing the uncoordinated entry, coordinating rudder with aileron and flying the remainder smoothly, without prompting. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to standardize the roll rate and coordinate the rudder so every pitch out is flown to the same smooth pattern.
texts_at.3: SP, due to a brief lag in coordinating rudder with the initial roll, controlled the aircraft in a smooth and solid way for nearly the whole pitch out, with roll, pitch and rudder inputs coordinated and the altitude held within 150 feet through the turn. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to standardize the roll rate and coordinate the rudder so every pitch out is flown to the same smooth pattern.

texts_above.1: SP flew the pitch out with the aircraft controlled smoothly for most of the turn, settling the coarse corrections after a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP flew the pitch out out of balance with a visible ball displacement at first before recognizing the uncoordinated entry, coordinating the rudder with the aileron and flying the remainder of the turn smoothly and firmly without prompting. Coordinating the rudder with the first roll input would remove that early ball displacement. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to assured roll-entry coordination technique.
texts_above.3: SP controlled the aircraft in a smooth and solid way throughout the pitch out, with roll, pitch and rudder inputs coordinated and the flight path continuous from entry to rollout. The coordination is already close through the entry; only the smallest lag remains to be removed. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to precise roll-entry coordination technique.
texts_above.4: SP flew the pitch out with control inputs of exceptional smoothness and precision, the aircraft tracking a continuous flight path with the ball centered throughout. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to first-rate roll-entry coordination technique.

texts.0: SP, due to reluctance to admit loss of visual contact and make the required call, did not handle the blind situation correctly when the leader was lost against the ground background in the pitch out. SP continued to turn toward the last known position of the leader with no call made and no deconfliction action taken. IP made the blind call and took the controls to separate the aircraft from the element.
texts.1: SP, due to hesitation in using the prescribed terminology once visual contact was lost, did not handle the blind situation in a timely manner. The blind call was made some five seconds late and only after IP prompted for it, and the deconfliction turn followed the call rather than accompanying it. Visual contact was regained, but the sequence was driven by IP direction.
texts.2: SP, due to visual contact being broken as the leader passed through the canopy bow during the pitch out, was momentarily blind in the turn. SP made the blind call promptly in the prescribed terminology, held the briefed altitude for deconfliction and regained visual contact before the rollout, with no IP intervention required.
texts.3: SP handled the blind situation correctly and in a timely manner when visual contact was momentarily lost during the pitch out. The call was made immediately in the prescribed terminology, the briefed deconfliction responsibilities were applied and visual contact was regained. The pattern sequence continued without disruption.
texts.4: SP handled the loss of visual contact with exemplary decisiveness, the blind call and the deconfliction action being taken in the same instant the leader was lost from sight. The call carried the position and altitude information needed for the leader to resolve the situation immediately. Visual contact was regained with negligible loss of pattern discipline.
texts.marginal: SP handled the blind situation within standards, but the call was made only after a perceptible pause and in phraseology that had to be repeated to be understood. The trend is a correct action taken with hesitation at exactly the moment when speed matters most. SP is expected to make the blind call immediately and in standard terminology as soon as visual contact is lost.

texts_at.0: SP flew the pitch out with the IP calling for the blind call to be made as soon as visual contact was lost. Making the blind call the instant visual contact is lost is a first exposure at this stage, so the call is not yet made without a cue. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to make the blind call immediately and in standard terminology as soon as visual contact is lost.
texts_at.1: SP, due to hesitation in using the prescribed terminology once visual contact was lost, made the blind call about five seconds late, with the deconfliction turn following the call rather than accompanying it and the altitude drifting 300 feet high at the tolerance limit, before visual contact was regained. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to make the blind call immediately and in standard terminology as soon as visual contact is lost.

error_modes.label: SPACING ASSESSMENT AND CORRECTION ON DOWNWIND

The interval remained far outside the briefed value with no correction attempted and the pattern sequence was compromised. IP had to direct the extension of the downwind leg and then take the controls to reestablish a usable interval.
texts.1: SP, due to situational awareness being reduced to the leader alone with no reference to the runway abeam position, did not assess the spacing after the pitch out. The interval finished at the limit of what the pattern allows and was corrected only after IP called for a power adjustment on the downwind leg. The correction restored the sequence but originated with IP.
texts.2: SP, due to the spacing check being delayed until well after the rollout, initially carried an interval noticeably shorter than the briefed one. SP detected the closure against the leader on the downwind leg, adjusted power and track in good time and restored the correct interval before the base turn, without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP assessed the spacing generated by the pitch out immediately on rolling out on downwind and maintained the briefed interval. The assessment was made against both the leader and the runway abeam position, and the small power adjustment required was applied early. The pattern sequence proceeded exactly as briefed.

error_modes.label: CLEARING NOT SACRIFICED TO PRECISE ALTITUDE OR AN EXACT 180 DEGREE TURN

texts.0: SP, due to the pitchout being flown to an exact 180 degrees and to a rigidly held altitude with the cross-check locked on the instruments, sacrificed clearing to maintain precise altitude control and an exact turn. The head stayed down from the roll-in to the rollout and nothing outside the aircraft was checked at any point of the maneuver. IP called the traffic in the pattern and took the controls to reestablish separation.
texts.1: SP, due to the exact 180 degrees of turn being treated as inviolable, sacrificed the lookout in order to hold the heading and the altitude precisely. The clearing scan was reduced to the bare minimum acceptable and was resumed only after IP called for the head to come up. Separation was never in doubt, but the priority was restored by IP and not by SP.
texts.2: SP, due to the altimeter being chased through the first quarter of the turn, initially let the clearing scan lapse in favour of precise altitude control. SP recognized the misplaced priority early, accepted a slight climb for energy management as the technique permits and kept the scan outside for the remainder of the pitchout, without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP did not sacrifice clearing to maintain precise altitude control or an exact 180 degree turn. Slight variations in altitude and in the degrees of turn were accepted for energy management and area orientation, exactly as the technique allows, while the parameters stayed inside tolerance. The pattern was cleared continuously through the maneuver.
texts.4: SP kept clearing as the first priority throughout the pitchout while still holding the altitude and the turn essentially on the briefed values. The degrees of turn were adjusted deliberately for area orientation and the small altitude variations accepted were explained on the debrief as energy management. Neither the lookout nor the parameters suffered.
texts.marginal: SP did not sacrifice clearing to precise altitude control within standards, but on every repetition the scan tightened noticeably as the heading approached the 180 degree point. The trend is a priority that reverses under the pressure of finishing the turn exactly. SP is expected to accept the small adjustments in altitude and degrees of turn that the technique permits and to keep the lookout continuous through the whole pitchout.

texts_at.0: SP flew the pitchout with the IP calling for the small altitude and heading adjustments the technique allows for energy management. Accepting the small variations in altitude and degrees of turn that the technique permits, rather than holding an exact value, is a first exposure at this stage, so the priority is not yet set without a cue. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance. SP is expected to accept the small adjustments in altitude and degrees of turn that the technique permits and keep the lookout continuous through the whole pitchout.
texts_at.1: SP, due to the exact 180 degrees of turn treated as inviolable, reduced the clearing scan to the bare minimum acceptable and let the altitude run out to 300 feet from the pattern value before the lookout was resumed. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to accept the small adjustments in altitude and degrees of turn that the technique permits and keep the lookout continuous through the whole pitchout.
texts_at.2: SP, due to the altimeter chased through the first quarter of the turn, let the clearing scan lapse in favour of precise altitude control at first before recognizing the misplaced priority early, accepting a climb of about 200 feet above the pattern altitude for energy management as the technique permits and keeping the scan outside for the remainder, without prompting. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to accept the small adjustments in altitude and degrees of turn that the technique permits and keep the lookout continuous through the whole pitchout.
texts_at.3: SP, due to a brief lapse of the clearing scan early in the turn, kept the lookout continuous through the turn while holding altitude within 150 feet and rolling out within 5 degrees of the briefed exit heading, accepting the variations in altitude and degrees of turn that the technique allows for energy management and area orientation. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to accept the small adjustments in altitude and degrees of turn that the technique permits and keep the lookout continuous through the whole pitchout.

texts_above.1: SP kept the lookout through most of the pitchout, reducing the clearing scan to the bare minimum before the head came up after a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP let the clearing scan lapse in favour of precise altitude control at first before recognizing the misplaced priority early, accepting a slight climb for energy management as the technique permits and keeping the scan outside for the remainder of the pitchout, without prompting. Recognizing the misplaced priority from the first quarter of the turn, rather than partway through, would remove that early lapse. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to competent clearing-priority discipline against precision.
texts_above.3: SP kept the lookout continuous through the pitchout while holding altitude and the turn near the briefed values, accepting only the slight variations that the technique allows for energy management and area orientation. The clearing priority is already held through most of the turn; only the smallest early lapse remains. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to disciplined clearing-priority discipline against precision.
texts_above.4: SP kept clearing as the first priority throughout the pitchout while still holding the altitude and the turn essentially on the briefed values, with the small deliberate adjustments explained on the debrief as energy management. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to faultless clearing-priority discipline against precision.

error_modes.label: DECELERATION WITH POWER AND SPEED BRAKE WHEN DIRECTED TO TAKE SPACING

texts.0: SP, due to the take spacing direction being answered with a maneuver alone and no power reduction or speed brake, did not generate any deceleration relative to Number 1. The range barely changed and the aircraft was still practically in the formation position when the leader expected a trail interval. IP reduced the power, extended the speed brake and built the required range.
texts.1: SP, due to the power being reduced in small steps rather than to a setting that would actually produce a deceleration, did not build the range at a usable rate after being directed to take spacing. The range was still short of the briefed one at the end of the maneuver and increased only after IP called for the speed brake. The interval was eventually achieved, but through IP prompting.
texts.2: SP, due to an initial power reduction that was insufficient for the range required, initially opened the interval more slowly than the briefed profile allowed. SP recognized the slow rate, added speed brake and completed the deceleration in good time, reaching the desired range and making the ready call without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP took spacing with a power reduction and speed brake used together, opening the range at a controlled rate to the briefed value. The deceleration was stopped as the desired range was reached, so the interval stabilized instead of continuing to grow. The aircraft was in trail at the briefed range for the rejoin.
texts.4: SP took spacing with a deceleration judged so accurately that the range stopped growing exactly at the briefed value. Power and speed brake were applied together and then reset, leaving the aircraft stabilized in trail with no overshoot. The interval was ideal for the rejoin that followed.
texts.marginal: SP took spacing within standards, but each time the deceleration was carried a little too far and the range finished at the outer edge of what the rejoin allows. The trend is a power reduction and speed brake extension that are removed late rather than anticipated. SP is expected to begin resetting the power before the desired range is reached so that the interval stabilizes on the briefed value.

texts_at.0: SP flew the deceleration for take spacing with the IP calling the power setting needed to build the range. Setting the power reduction to the profile from the first movement is a first exposure at this stage, so the deceleration rate is not yet set without a cue. The Training Section still expects IP assistance for this maneuver at this point. SP is expected to begin resetting the power before the desired range is reached so the interval stabilizes on the briefed value.
texts_at.1: SP, due to the power reduced in small steps rather than to a setting that would actually produce a deceleration, finished the maneuver with the range still short of the briefed one and the airspeed still 20 knots fast, at the limit of the tolerance, before it increased with the speed brake called for. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to begin resetting the power before the desired range is reached so the interval stabilizes on the briefed value.
texts_at.2: SP, due to an initial power reduction insufficient for the range required, opened the interval more slowly than the briefed profile allowed at first, with the airspeed about 15 knots off the deceleration figure, before recognizing the slow rate, adding speed brake and completing the deceleration in good time, reaching the desired range and making the ready call without prompting. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to begin resetting the power before the desired range is reached so the interval stabilizes on the briefed value.
texts_at.3: SP, due to a brief lag before the deceleration rate matched the briefed profile, took spacing with a power reduction and speed brake used together, opening the range at a controlled rate and holding the airspeed within 10 knots of the briefed deceleration figure as the desired range was reached. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to begin resetting the power before the desired range is reached so the interval stabilizes on the briefed value.

texts_above.2: SP opened the interval more slowly than the briefed profile allowed at first before recognizing the slow rate, adding speed brake and completing the deceleration in good time, reaching the desired range and making the ready call without prompting. Setting the power reduction to the profile from the first movement, rather than adding to it, would remove that slow start. texts_above.3: SP took spacing with a power reduction and speed brake used together, opening the range at a controlled rate to the briefed value, with the deceleration stopped as the desired range was reached so the interval stabilized. The deceleration rate already matches the briefed profile closely; only the smallest further margin remains. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to very good take-spacing deceleration judgment.
texts_above.4: SP took spacing with a deceleration judged so accurately that the range stopped growing exactly at the briefed value, power and speed brake applied together and then reset with no overshoot. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to excellent take-spacing deceleration judgment.

error_modes.label: S TURNS FOR SPACING BEHIND AND BELOW NUMBER 1 PROP WASH

texts.0: SP, due to the S turns for spacing being flown level with and directly behind Number 1, did not keep the maneuver behind and below the leader prop wash. The aircraft was flown through the wash repeatedly, with sharp uncommanded rolls each time and the leader lost from view during the disturbance. IP took the controls, descended clear of the wash and reestablished a stable trail position.
texts.1: SP, due to the vertical displacement below the leader being allowed to wash out as the S turns developed, did not keep clear of Number 1 prop wash. The aircraft clipped the wash on each reversal and the position was corrected only after IP called for a descent. Spacing was achieved, but the whole maneuver was flown on the edge of the wash and the correction came from IP.
texts.2: SP, due to the first S turn being started before descending below the leader, initially flew into the edge of the prop wash and felt a light roll disturbance. SP eased the aircraft lower at once and flew the remaining reversals behind and below Number 1 as the technique describes, completing the spacing maneuver without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP took spacing with a series of S turns flown behind and below Number 1 prop wash, keeping the aircraft clear of the disturbance throughout. Each reversal was made with visual contact on the leader retained and the range building steadily. The desired interval was reached with the aircraft stable.
texts.4: SP flew the S turns for spacing precisely behind and below the leader, never entering the prop wash and never losing the visual on Number 1. The reversals were smooth and symmetric and the range grew at an even rate to the briefed value. The technique was applied exactly as described.
texts.marginal: SP kept the S turns behind and below Number 1 within standards, but the aircraft skimmed the top of the prop wash on the reversals and the resulting jolts were absorbed rather than avoided. The trend is a vertical offset that is only just sufficient and shrinks as the maneuver progresses. SP is expected to establish and hold a clear displacement below the leader wash before starting the S turns.

texts_at.0: SP flew the S turns for spacing with the IP calling for the aircraft to be eased below the leader before the first reversal. Establishing a clear displacement below the leader's wash before starting the S turns is a first exposure at this stage, so the displacement is not yet held without a cue. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to establish and hold a clear displacement below the leader wash before starting the S turns.
texts_at.1: SP, due to the vertical displacement below the leader allowed to wash out as the S turns developed, clipped the wash on each reversal before the position was corrected with a descent. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to establish and hold a clear displacement below the leader wash before starting the S turns.
texts_at.2: SP, due to the first S turn started before descending below the leader, flew into the edge of the prop wash at first with a light roll disturbance before easing the aircraft lower at once and flying the remaining reversals behind and below Number 1 as the technique describes, without prompting. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to establish and hold a clear displacement below the leader wash before starting the S turns.
texts_at.3: SP, due to a brief lag before the aircraft was eased below the leader, took spacing with a series of S turns flown behind and below Number 1 prop wash, keeping the aircraft clear of the disturbance throughout, each reversal made with visual contact retained. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to establish and hold a clear displacement below the leader wash before starting the S turns.

texts_above.1: SP flew the S turns for spacing, clipping the prop wash on each reversal before the position was corrected with a descent after a verbal call from the IP. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP flew into the edge of the prop wash at first with a light roll disturbance before easing the aircraft lower at once and flying the remaining reversals behind and below Number 1 as the technique describes, without prompting. Descending below the leader before the first reversal, rather than during it, would remove that early disturbance. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound prop-wash clearance discipline in S turns.

The vertical offset is already held clear of the wash for most of the maneuver; only the smallest early margin remains. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to sure-handed prop-wash clearance discipline in S turns.
texts_above.4: SP flew the S turns for spacing precisely behind and below the leader, never entering the prop wash and never losing the visual on Number 1, with the reversals smooth and symmetric. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exceptional prop-wash clearance discipline in S turns.
